Good morning everyone.

In the previous section, we learned what a DBMS is and why it is important.

Now I will explain how we design a database before actually creating it. Two important concepts in this process are the Entity Relationship model and the Relational model.

Let's begin with the Entity Relationship model, also called the ER model.

The ER model is used to represent the structure of a database visually. It helps database designers understand what information needs to be stored and how different types of information are connected.

The three basic components of an ER model are entities, attributes, and relationships.

First, let's understand entities.

An entity is a real-world object or concept about which we want to store information.

For example, in a college database, Student, Teacher, Course, and Department can all be entities.

An entity type describes a category of objects, while an entity instance represents one particular object in that category.

For example, Student is an entity type, and a particular student with roll number 101 is an entity instance.

The second component is attributes.

Attributes describe the properties of an entity.

For example, a Student entity may have attributes such as Student_ID, Name, Age, Email, and Department.

Attributes can be of different types.

A simple attribute cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts. For example, Age.

A composite attribute can be divided into smaller components. For example, Address may contain Street, City, State, and PIN code.

A single-valued attribute has only one value for an entity, such as a date of birth.

A multivalued attribute can have multiple values. For example, a student may have multiple phone numbers.

A derived attribute can be calculated from another attribute. For example, Age can be calculated using Date of Birth.

The third component is relationships.

A relationship describes how two or more entities are associated with each other.

For example, a Student enrolls in a Course. Here, Student and Course are entities, and Enrolls is the relationship.

Relationships are commonly classified based on cardinality.

One-to-one means one entity is associated with only one entity on the other side.

One-to-many means one entity can be associated with many entities. For example, one department can have many students.

Many-to-many means many entities on one side can be associated with many entities on the other side. For example, many students can enroll in many courses.

In ER diagrams, entities are generally represented using rectangles, attributes using ovals, and relationships using diamonds. Lines connect these components.

Another important concept is the key.

A key is an attribute, or a group of attributes, used to identify records or establish relationships between tables.

A super key is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a record.

A candidate key is a minimal super key, meaning no unnecessary attribute is included.

A primary key is the candidate key selected to identify each record in a table.

For example, in a Student table, Student_ID can be selected as the primary key because every student has a unique ID.

A foreign key is an attribute in one table that refers to a key in another table. It helps establish relationships between tables.

For example, a Department_ID in the Student table may refer to Department_ID in the Department table.

Now let's move to the Relational model.

The relational model represents data in the form of tables. Each table is also called a relation.

A table consists of rows and columns.

A row is called a tuple, and a column is called an attribute.

For example, imagine a Student table containing Student_ID, Name, and Department_ID.

One row might contain the information: 101, Rahul, and 10.

Another row might contain: 102, Priya, and 20.

Each row represents one student, and each column represents one property of the student.

The relational model is powerful because it allows us to connect information stored in different tables.

For example, instead of storing the department name repeatedly for every student, we can create a separate Department table.

The Student table stores Department_ID as a foreign key, and the Department table stores the corresponding department name.

This avoids unnecessary repetition and makes database management easier.

Now let's understand relational integrity constraints.

Integrity constraints are rules that help maintain the correctness of data.

Entity integrity means that a primary key cannot contain NULL values because every record must be identifiable.

Referential integrity means that a foreign key value must refer to an existing valid record in the referenced table, unless NULL is permitted.

Domain constraints ensure that values belong to an allowed domain. For example, Age may be restricted to positive integers.

These constraints prevent invalid information from entering the database.

To summarize, the ER model helps us plan and visually design the database, while the relational model helps us represent that design using tables, rows, columns, and keys.

Together, these concepts provide the foundation for creating a well-structured database.

In the next section, my teammate will explain SQL, which is the language used to interact with relational databases.

Thank you.
